14: # Skill Reference File Templates - AI Agent Skills
15: 
16: Templates for creating reference files in AI agent skills with deep-dive technical guidance.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Location & Naming
23: 
24: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/references/`
25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only
27: 
28: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
29: |---------------|-----------------|
30: | `implementation-workflows.md` | `ImplementationWorkflows.md` (PascalCase) |
31: | `tool-catalog.md` | `tool_catalog.md` (snake_case) |
32: | `debugging-guide.md` | `DebuggingGuide.MD` (wrong case) |
33: | `quick-reference.md` | `quickReference.md` (camelCase) |
34: | `code-quality-standards.md` | `code quality standards.md` (spaces) |
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
69: 
70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.
72: 
73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95: 
96: #### BAD Intro Structure (duplicates content)
97: 
98: ```markdown
99: # Git Commit Workflows
100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
104: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
108: 
109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Intro vs Section 1 Content Placement
121: 
122: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | Section 1 OVERVIEW |
123: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ |
124: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat) |
125: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
126: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
127: | Primary Sources       | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (as "Key Sources") |
128: | Purpose (detailed)    | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
129: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES              |
130: | Any H3 subsections    | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES              |
131: 
132: ---
133: 
134: ### Reference Body Skeleton
135: 
136: **Every reference body follows this order.** The hook and the Purpose say different things: the hook names the job, and the Purpose names the outcome.
137: 
138: ```markdown
139: # [Title]
140: 
141: [1-2 sentence hook: what this reference covers and when to reach for it.]
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 1. OVERVIEW
146: 
147: ### Purpose
148: 
149: [The outcome this reference produces, in one or two sentences.]
150: 
151: ### When to Use
152: 
153: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
154: - [Second trigger]
155: 
156: ### Core Principle
157: 
158: [One-line statement that governs every rule below.]
159: 
160: ### Boundaries
161: 
162: - **In scope**: [What this reference owns]
163: - **Out of scope**: [What belongs in a sibling reference]
164: 
165: ### Key Sources
166: 
167: - [title](url) - [What the source establishes]
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 2. [CONTENT SECTION]
172: 
173: ### [Rule Group]
174: 
175: - **Rule:** [What to do]
176: - **Why:** [The failure it prevents]
177: - **Check:** [How to verify it]
178: 
179: ---
180: 
181: ## 3. [CONTENT SECTION]
182: 
183: [Body of the section]
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 4. RELATED RESOURCES
188: 
189: - [title](./sibling-reference.md) - [What the reader gets there]
190: ```
191: 
192: **Rules the skeleton encodes:**
193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.
194: - Content sections use integer numbers only: `## 2.`, `## 3.`, and so on.
195: - Rule fields are `- **Label:** text` bullets, never two bold labels on consecutive lines.
196: - Links are `[title](url)`, never a bare URL.
197: - Every `---` has a blank line above it, so a divider never turns the line above into a setext heading.
198: - A related section, when present, is the last H2.
199: 
200: ---

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 3. WHEN TO CREATE REFERENCE FILES
235: 
236: ### Create Reference File When
237: 
238: **Workflow Complexity**:
239: - Multi-phase workflows with validation checkpoints
240: - Decision trees with multiple branches
241: - Pattern libraries with 5+ variations
242: - Systematic debugging procedures
243: 
244: **Technical Depth**:
245: - Root cause analysis required
246: - Tool integration details (MCP, scripts)
247: - Before/after code transformations
248: - Common error patterns and fixes
249: 
250: **Size Threshold**:
251: - Content exceeds 200 lines
252: - Multiple related workflows
253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed
254: 
255: ### Keep in SKILL.md When
256: 
257: **Core Content**:
258: - Overview and "When to Use"
259: - High-level workflow (3-5 steps)
260: - Essential rules (ALWAYS/NEVER/ESCALATE IF)
261:   > **Note**: RULES sections in SKILL.md use ALL-CAPS H3 headers: `### ALWAYS`, `### NEVER`, `### ESCALATE IF` (or `####` at phase depth). See [skill-md-template.md](./skill-md-template.md) for the complete pattern.
262: - Quick reference
263: 
264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines
265: 
266: ### Reference File Types for AI Agent Skills
267: 
268: | Type                | Purpose                                | Example (kebab-case)          | Size           |
269: | ------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------- |
270: | **Workflow**        | Multi-phase processes with checkpoints | `implementation-workflows.md` | 500-1500 lines |
271: | **Pattern Library** | Code patterns with before/after        | `shared-patterns.md`          | 300-800 lines  |
272: | **Standards**       | Rules and conventions                  | `code-quality-standards.md`   | 400-1000 lines |
273: | **Debugging**       | Systematic troubleshooting             | `debugging-workflows.md`      | 600-1200 lines |
274: | **Tool Guide**      | MCP/external tool integration          | `devtools-guide.md`           | 200-600 lines  |
275: | **Quick Reference** | Commands, shortcuts, checklists        | `quick-reference.md`          | 200-400 lines  |
276: 
277: **Note:** All authored reference file names use kebab-case (hyphens, lowercase).
278:

281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
300: 
301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```
305: 
306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"
309: - "Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history"
310: 
311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312: 
313: **Purpose**: Structured processes with mandatory checkpoints
314: 
315: **Format**:
316: ```markdown
317: ### The [Number] Phases
318: 
319: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
320:

322: 
323: **Purpose**: [What this phase accomplishes]
324:

326: 1. [Action 1]
327: 2. [Action 2]
328: 
329: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`
330: 
331: #### Phase 2: [Phase Name]
332: 
333: [Similar structure]
334: ```

336: **Key Elements**:
337: - **"You MUST complete"** - Mandatory language
338: - **Named checkpoints** - `checkpoint_name` for validation
339: - **Sequential phases** - Cannot skip ahead

341: ### Before/After Code Examples
342: 
343: **Purpose**: Show transformation from wrong to right
344: 
345: **Format**:
346: ```markdown

348:

354: 
355: **AFTER**: [Solution description]

359: \```
360: 
361: **Why better**: [Explanation of improvement]
362: ```
363: 
364: **Key Elements**:
365: - `BEFORE:` marker for the wrong-way code
366: - `AFTER:` marker for the right-way code
367: - Inline comments explaining issues
368: - "Why better" rationale

371: 
372: **Purpose**: Compare approaches across scenarios
373: 
374: **Format**:

381: | [Scenario 2] | [Wrong way]        | [Right way]        | [Rationale] |

384: **Use when**: Multiple scenarios need comparison

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882: 
883: ---
884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006: 
1007: ---
1008: 
1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"
1073:

21: 
22: ### Location & Naming

25: 
26: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with `.md` extension only

38: ## 2. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
39: 
40: ### Document Structure: Title and Intro
41: 
42: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
43: 
44: ```markdown
45: ---
46: title: [Title]
47: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
48: trigger_phrases:
49:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
50:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
51:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
52: importance_tier: normal
53: contextType: general
54: version: 1.0.0.0
55: ---
56: 
57: # [Title]
58: 
59: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: \## 1. OVERVIEW
64: [All detailed content goes here, NOT in the intro]
65: 
66: ```
67: 
68: Every reference file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content. `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, with `important` only for formal contract docs. `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.

70: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and Section 1.**
71: > The intro is a hook. Section 1 provides the details.

73: #### GOOD Intro Structure
74: 
75: ```markdown
76: # Git Commit Workflows
77: 
78: This reference turns a mixed working tree into a small set of reviewable commits.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: \## 1. OVERVIEW
83: 
84: ### Purpose
85: Each rule keeps one commit focused on one intent, so history stays easy to read, review and revert.
86: 
87: ### When to Use
88: - Creating commits with multiple file changes
89: - Filtering generated files from commits
90: - Writing clear commit messages
91: 
92: ### Core Principle
93: Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history.
94: ```
95:

98: ```markdown

100: 
101: Step-by-step workflows for creating clean, atomic commits with proper filtering.
102: 
103: ### Core Principle   ← WRONG: No headers in intro!

105: 
106: ### When to Use      ← WRONG: This belongs in Section 1!
107: - Creating commits with multiple file changes

109: ---
110: 
111: \## 1. OVERVIEW
112: 
113: ### Purpose
114: Provides systematic workflows...  ← Now this duplicates the intro!
115: 
116: ### Core Principle
117: Atomic commits...  ← DUPLICATED from intro!

193: - Core Principle, Boundaries and Key Sources follow Purpose and When to Use, in that order, and each appears only when it has content.

202: ### What Are AI Agent Skill Reference Files?
203: 
204: Reference files are detailed technical documentation in the `references/` directory that provide deep-dive guidance with **explicit reasoning** - making thought processes visible, showing decision logic, and analyzing root causes.
205: 
206: **Core Purpose**:
207: - **Technical depth** - Step-by-step reasoning with rationale
208: - **Phased workflows** - Structured processes with validation checkpoints
209: - **Pattern libraries** - Before/after examples, comparison tables
210: - **Tool integration** - MCP tools, scripts, asset references
211: - **Root cause analysis** - Systematic debugging and troubleshooting
212: 
213: **Key Difference from Generic Documentation**:
214: - AI agent skills = Actionable workflows with explicit reasoning
215: - Generic docs = Information reference without decision logic
216: 
217: ### Progressive Disclosure in Skills
218: 
219: ```
220: Level 1: Metadata (name + description)
221:          └─ Always in context (~100 words)
222:             ↓
223: Level 2: SKILL.md body
224:          └─ When skill triggers (<5k words)
225:             ↓
226: Level 3: Reference files (this document)
227:          └─ Loaded as needed (500-3000 lines per file)
228: ```
229: 
230: **Reference files = Level 3**: Deep technical guidance loaded only when the agent needs specific workflow details.

245: - Root cause analysis required

253: - Extensive troubleshooting needed

262: - Quick reference

264: **Size**: Content under 200 lines

281: ## 4. AI AGENT SKILL REFERENCE CHARACTERISTICS
282: 
283: ### Core Principle Statements
284: 
285: **Purpose**: Distill philosophy into one-line wisdom
286: 
287: > **PLACEMENT**: Core Principle goes in **Section 1 OVERVIEW**, NOT in the intro paragraph after the H1 title.
288: 
289: **Format**:
290: ```markdown
291: \## 1. OVERVIEW
292: 
293: ### Purpose
294: 
295: [The outcome this reference produces]
296: 
297: ### When to Use
298: 
299: - [Trigger that sends a reader here]
300: 
301: ### Core Principle
302: 
303: [Single powerful statement that captures the workflow's essence]
304: ```
305: 
306: **Examples from Real Skills**:
307: - "Wait for the actual condition you care about, not a guess about how long it takes"
308: - "ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure"
309: - "Atomic commits with clear intent + filtered artifacts = maintainable Git history"
310: 
311: ### Phased Workflows with Validation
312: 
313: **Purpose**: Structured processes with mandatory checkpoints
314: 
315: **Format**:
316: ```markdown
317: ### The [Number] Phases
318: 
319: You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.
320: 
321: #### Phase 1: [Phase Name]
322: 
323: **Purpose**: [What this phase accomplishes]
324: 
325: **Actions**:
326: 1. [Action 1]
327: 2. [Action 2]
328: 
329: **Validation**: `checkpoint_name`

332: 
333: [Similar structure]
334: ```

337: - **"You MUST complete"** - Mandatory language
338: - **Named checkpoints** - `checkpoint_name` for validation
339: - **Sequential phases** - Cannot skip ahead

682: ## 5. CONVERTING LOGIC TO EXECUTABLE CODE
683: 
684: ### When to Extract Logic from Markdown
685: 
686: **Purpose**: Separate documentation from executable code for better maintainability, testability, and reusability.
687: 
688: **Decision Criteria**:
689: 
690: | Pattern Type          | Keep in Markdown  | Extract to Code           | Reasoning                                    |
691: | --------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
692: | **Python functions**  | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/scripts/*.py`   | Type safety, unit testing, reusability       |
693: | **YAML configs**      | ❌ No              | ✅ Yes → `/assets/*.yaml`  | Dynamic loading, version control, validation |
694: | **Decision trees**    | ⚠️ High-level only | ✅ Details → YAML + Python | Machine-readable, can be validated           |
695: | **Command mappings**  | ⚠️ Examples only   | ✅ Full map → YAML         | Easier maintenance, can be imported          |
696: | **Workflow diagrams** | ✅ Yes (generated) | ✅ Source → YAML           | YAML = source of truth, diagram = output     |
697: | **Checklists**        | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Human-readable is primary use case           |
698: | **Before/after code** | ✅ Yes             | ❌ No                      | Educational, not executable                  |
699: 
700: ### Extraction Pattern
701: 
702: **In Markdown (Reference File)**:
703: ```markdown
704: ### [Workflow Name]
705: 
706: [High-level description of what the workflow does]
707: 
708: **Implementation:** See [workflow_name.py](../scripts/workflow_name.py) for execution logic and [workflow-config.yaml](../assets/workflow-config.yaml) for configuration.
709: 
710: **Quick Overview**:
711: 1. [Step 1 - high level]
712: 2. [Step 2 - high level]
713: 3. [Step 3 - high level]
714: 
715: **Configuration Options:**
716: - See YAML config for customizable parameters
717: - Default values optimized for common use cases
718: ```
719: 
720: ### Benefits of Separation
721: 
722: - **Type safety** - Python type hints catch errors at development time
723: - **Testability** - Unit tests for logic, integration tests for workflows
724: - **Reusability** - Imported by multiple skills or scripts
725: - **Version control** - Git diffs show logic changes clearly
726: - **Schema validation** - YAML can be validated against schemas
727: - **Dynamic loading** - Configuration changes without code edits
728: 
729: ### Example: Mode Detection Extraction
730: 
731: **❌ BEFORE** (inline Python in markdown):
732: \```python
733: def detect_mode(request):
734:     if '$quick' in request: return 'quick', 5
735:     elif '$ticket' in request: return 'ticket', 10
736:     return 'interactive', 10
737: \```
738: 
739: **✅ AFTER** (extracted with type safety):
740: 
741: `/scripts/mode_detection.py`:
742: \```python
743: from dataclasses import dataclass
744: 
745: @dataclass
746: class ModeConfig:
747:     mode: str
748:     depth_rounds: int
749: 
750: def detect_mode(request: str) -> ModeConfig:
751:     """Detect mode from command shortcuts."""
752:     if '$quick' in request:
753:         return ModeConfig('quick', 5)
754:     elif '$ticket' in request:
755:         return ModeConfig('ticket', 10)
756:     return ModeConfig('interactive', 10)
757: \```
758: 
759: `/tests/test_mode_detection.py`:
760: \```python
761: def test_quick_mode():
762:     assert detect_mode("$quick fix").mode == 'quick'
763: \```
764: 
765: **Why better:** Type hints, testable, reusable, separated from docs
766:

769: ## 6. YAML CONFIGURATION PATTERNS
770: 
771: ### Purpose
772: 
773: **YAML for configuration data** - Separate configuration from documentation for easier maintenance and dynamic loading.
774: 
775: **When to use YAML**:
776: - Configuration data (thresholds, mappings, rules)
777: - Data structures (nested objects, lists)
778: - Workflow definitions (step sequences, pipelines)
779: - Decision trees (conditional logic patterns)
780: - Validation schemas
781: 
782: ### Standard YAML Structure
783: 
784: ```yaml
785: # [config-name].yaml
786: metadata:
787:   version: "1.0.0"
788:   description: "Configuration for [feature name]"
789: 
790: config:
791:   threshold_values:
792:     low: 1
793:     medium: 5
794:     high: 10
795:   feature_flags:
796:     enable_feature_x: true
797:   mappings:
798:     $quick: "quick_mode"
799:     $ticket: "ticket_mode"
800: ```
801: 
802: ### File Organization
803: 
804: ```
805: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
806: ├── assets/
807: │   ├── workflow-configs/
808: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
809: │   │   ├── variant-detection.yaml
810: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
811: │   ├── mappings/
812: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
813: │   │   ├── mode-recognition.yaml
814: │   │   └── shortcut-definitions.yaml
815: │   └── templates/
816: │       └── [template files]
817: ```
818: 
819: ### Loading Pattern (Python)
820: 
821: ```python
822: import yaml
823: from pathlib import Path
824: 
825: def load_config(config_name: str) -> dict:
826:     """Load YAML config from assets directory."""
827:     config_path = Path(__file__).parent.parent / f"assets/{config_name}.yaml"
828:     with open(config_path) as f:
829:         return yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
830: 
831: # Usage
832: config = load_config("canvas-methodology")
833: ```
834: 
835: ### Example: Variant Detection Rules
836: 
837: **❌ BEFORE** (markdown table):
838: ```markdown
839: | Trigger                    | Action             |
840: | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
841: | "show options"             | Offer 3-5 variants |
842: | Complexity 7+ + "not sure" | Offer variants     |
843: ```
844: 
845: **✅ AFTER** (YAML + Python):
846: 
847: `/assets/variant-detection-rules.yaml`:
848: ```yaml
849: config:
850:   variant_triggers:
851:     explicit_keywords: ["show me options", "variations"]
852:     implicit:
853:       complexity_threshold: 7
854:       uncertainty_signals: ["not sure", "what would work"]
855:   variant_count:
856:     simple: [2, 3]
857:     complex: [5, 10]
858: ```
859: 
860: `/scripts/variant_detector.py`:
861: ```python
862: import yaml
863: 
864: class VariantDetector:
865:     def __init__(self, config_path: str):
866:         with open(config_path) as f:
867:             self.config = yaml.safe_load(f)['config']
868: 
869:     def should_generate_variants(self, request: str, complexity: int) -> bool:
870:         keywords = self.config['variant_triggers']['explicit_keywords']
871:         if any(kw in request.lower() for kw in keywords):
872:             return True
873: 
874:         threshold = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['complexity_threshold']
875:         if complexity >= threshold:
876:             signals = self.config['variant_triggers']['implicit']['uncertainty_signals']
877:             return any(s in request.lower() for s in signals)
878:         return False
879: ```
880: 
881: **Why better:** Dynamic config loading, easier maintenance, schema validation possible
882:

884: 
885: ## 7. PYTHON SCRIPT INTEGRATION
886: 
887: ### When to Use Python for Logic
888: 
889: **Use Python scripts when**:
890: - Procedural logic (workflows, algorithms)
891: - Complex conditionals (multi-step decisions)
892: - Data transformation (processing, validation)
893: - API integration (external services)
894: - File operations (reading, parsing, generating)
895: 
896: ### Type Hints and Docstring Standards
897: 
898: **Always include**:
899: - Type hints for parameters and return values
900: - Google-style docstrings (Args, Returns, Raises, Examples)
901: - Dataclasses for structured data
902: 
903: **Example**:
904: ```python
905: from dataclasses import dataclass
906: from pathlib import Path
907: 
908: @dataclass
909: class ValidationResult:
910:     is_valid: bool
911:     errors: list[str]
912: 
913: def validate_config(config_path: Path) -> ValidationResult:
914:     """
915:     Validate configuration file.
916: 
917:     Args:
918:         config_path: Path to YAML config file
919: 
920:     Returns:
921:         ValidationResult with status and errors
922: 
923:     Raises:
924:         FileNotFoundError: If config doesn't exist
925:     """
926:     if not config_path.exists():
927:         raise FileNotFoundError(f"Config not found: {config_path}")
928:     # Validation logic
929:     return ValidationResult(is_valid=True, errors=[])
930: ```
931: 
932: ### Unit Testing Requirements
933: 
934: **Every Python script must have tests**:
935: - Naming: `test_[script_name].py` in `/tests/` directory
936: - Coverage: ≥80% line coverage
937: - Framework: pytest
938: 
939: **Example**:
940: ```python
941: import pytest
942: from scripts.config_validator import validate_config
943: 
944: def test_validate_success(tmp_path):
945:     config = tmp_path / "config.yaml"
946:     config.write_text("config:\n  threshold: 5")
947:     result = validate_config(config)
948:     assert result.is_valid
949: 
950: def test_validate_missing_file():
951:     with pytest.raises(FileNotFoundError):
952:         validate_config(Path("nonexistent.yaml"))
953: ```
954: 
955: ### Import and Reference Patterns
956: 
957: **Python import order**: Standard library → Third-party → Local
958: 
959: **Markdown references**:
960: ```markdown
961: **See also:** [script_name.py](../scripts/script_name.py), [config.yaml](../assets/config.yaml)
962: ```
963: 
964: ### Example: Workflow Decision Logic
965: 
966: **❌ BEFORE** (text decision tree):
967: ```markdown
968: IF "$quick": use quick mode (5 rounds)
969: IF "$ticket": use ticket mode (10 rounds)
970: OTHERWISE: use interactive mode
971: ```
972: 
973: **✅ AFTER** (Python with type safety):
974: 
975: `/scripts/workflow_router.py`:
976: ```python
977: from typing import Literal
978: from dataclasses import dataclass
979: 
980: WorkflowMode = Literal["quick", "ticket", "interactive"]
981: 
982: @dataclass
983: class WorkflowDecision:
984:     mode: WorkflowMode
985:     depth_rounds: int
986: 
987: def route_workflow(request: str) -> WorkflowDecision:
988:     """Route request to appropriate workflow."""
989:     if '$quick' in request.lower():
990:         return WorkflowDecision("quick", 5)
991:     if '$ticket' in request.lower():
992:         return WorkflowDecision("ticket", 10)
993:     return WorkflowDecision("interactive", 10)
994: ```
995: 
996: `/tests/test_workflow_router.py`:
997: ```python
998: def test_quick_mode():
999:     assert route_workflow("$quick fix").mode == "quick"
1000: 
1001: def test_default_mode():
1002:     assert route_workflow("help me").mode == "interactive"
1003: ```
1004: 
1005: **Why better:** Type-safe with Literal, testable, structured with dataclass
1006:

1009: ## 8. STANDARD STRUCTURE TEMPLATE
1010: 
1011: ### Complete Skill Directory Structure
1012: 
1013: **Path:** `.skilled/skills/` (singular, not `skills` or `openskills`)
1014: 
1015: ```
1016: .skilled/skills/[skill-name]/
1017: ├── SKILL.md                    # Main skill file (Level 2 in progressive disclosure)
1018: ├── references/                 # Deep-dive technical documentation (Level 3)
1019: │   ├── workflow-name.md        # Multi-phase workflows with checkpoints (kebab-case)
1020: │   ├── patterns-library.md     # Before/after code patterns (kebab-case)
1021: │   ├── debugging-guide.md      # Systematic troubleshooting (kebab-case)
1022: │   └── quick-reference.md      # Commands, shortcuts, checklists (kebab-case)
1023: ├── scripts/                    # Executable Python logic
1024: │   ├── mode_detection.py       # Procedural logic, algorithms
1025: │   ├── workflow_router.py      # Decision logic
1026: │   ├── config_validator.py     # Data transformation
1027: │   └── __init__.py             # Package initialization
1028: ├── assets/                     # Configuration and data files
1029: │   ├── workflow-configs/       # YAML workflow definitions
1030: │   │   ├── canvas-methodology.yaml
1031: │   │   └── complexity-scoring.yaml
1032: │   ├── mappings/               # YAML mapping data
1033: │   │   ├── command-mappings.yaml
1034: │   │   └── mode-recognition.yaml
1035: │   └── templates/              # Markdown/code templates
1036: │       ├── template-name.md
1037: │       └── component-template.tsx
1038: └── tests/                      # Unit and integration tests
1039:     ├── test_mode_detection.py
1040:     ├── test_workflow_router.py
1041:     ├── test_config_validator.py
1042:     └── __init__.py
1043: ```
1044: 
1045: ### Directory Purposes
1046: 
1047: **SKILL.md** (Required): Overview, workflow (3-5 steps), rules. Target: <200 lines
1048: 
1049: **references/** (Optional): Detailed workflows, patterns, debugging. Target: 500-3000 lines/file. **All authored filenames must use kebab-case.**
1050: 
1051: **scripts/** (Optional): Python logic - procedural, routing, validation. Requires type hints, tests
1052: 
1053: **assets/** (Optional): YAML configs, workflow definitions, templates, mappings
1054: 
1055: **tests/** (Required if scripts/ exists): Unit tests with ≥80% coverage, pytest, `test_[name].py`
1056: 
1057: ### When to Create Each Directory
1058: 
1059: | Directory     | Create When                                                     | Don't Create When                           |
1060: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
1061: | `references/` | Content >200 lines, multi-phase workflows, systematic debugging | Simple skills <200 lines total              |
1062: | `scripts/`    | Python logic extracted from markdown, reusable functions        | Pure documentation, no executable logic     |
1063: | `assets/`     | YAML configs, templates, structured data                        | No configuration data, inline examples only |
1064: | `tests/`      | `scripts/` directory exists                                     | No Python scripts to test                   |
1065: 
1066: ### Integration Pattern
1067: 
1068: **How components work together:**
1069: - SKILL.md references scripts: `[workflow_router.py](./scripts/workflow_router.py)`
1070: - Scripts load configs: `yaml.safe_load(f"../assets/config.yaml")`
1071: - Tests verify scripts: `assert route_workflow("input").mode == "expected"`
1072: - Markdown links to all: "See [script.py](../scripts/), [config.yaml](../assets/)"

15: # Visual Hierarchy
16: 
17: The technique that does the most visible work. `SKILL.md` names its four rules; this is the full method, the values behind them, and the cases where it gets counterintuitive.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Core Principle
24: 
25: A design looks designed because things are ranked, not because they are styled. When everything competes, the interface reads as noise no matter how good the individual values are.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Nothing on the screen draws the eye, or everything does.
30: - One element will not stand out no matter what is added to it.
31: - Deciding how to style an action, especially a destructive one.
32: - Data reads like a database dump.
33: - An icon or a border is fighting the text next to it.
34: 
35: ### The Three Tiers
36: 
37: Everything on screen sits in a pyramid: **primary**, **secondary**, **tertiary**. Assign every element to a tier before styling any of them. An element that cannot be assigned is usually one that should not be on the screen.
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. CARRY EMPHASIS WITH WEIGHT AND COLOR
42: 
43: **Size is not everything.** Leaning on font size alone produces primary content that is too big and secondary content that is too small — the classic symptom of a hierarchy built with one lever. Carry emphasis with **weight** and **color** instead, and keep sizes near the middle of the scale.
44: 
45: **Three text colors, maximum:**
46: 
47: - dark for primary content
48: - grey for secondary content
49: - lighter grey for tertiary content such as footnotes and copyright
50: 
51: All three carry real body-size text, so all three need 4.5:1. "Lighter grey" means the lightest shade that still clears it — roughly the middle of a nine-step ramp, not the pale end. The pale shades are for disabled states and large text only. The per-step mapping is in [`../assets/token-starter-set.md`](../assets/token-starter-set.md) Section 4.
52: 
53: A fourth text color is almost always a tier that was never decided.
54: 
55: ---
56: 
57: ## 3. EMPHASIZE BY DE-EMPHASIZING
58: 
59: When the important element will not stand out and there is nothing left to add to it, the problem is not the element. It is the competition.
60: 
61: Soften what competes instead: fade the inactive nav items, drop the sidebar's background color so the main content sits forward, reduce the weight of the repeated metadata on every row. The primary element gets more prominent without changing at all.
62: 
63: This is the single highest-yield move in the whole skill, and it is counterintuitive enough that most people reach for amplification first and end up with a screen where everything shouts.
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 4. ACTIONS
68: 
69: **Style actions by hierarchy, not by semantics.**
70: 
71: | Tier | Treatment | Count |
72: |---|---|---|
73: | Primary | Solid, high contrast | Usually exactly one per page |
74: | Secondary | Outline, or a low-contrast background | As many as the page genuinely needs |
75: | Tertiary | Styled like a link | The rest |
76: 
77: **Destructive does not mean a big red button.** The instinct is to style by what the action *means*; the rule is to style by what it *ranks*. If "Delete" is not the primary action on the page — and on a list or detail view it almost never is — give it tertiary treatment.
78: 
79: Then make it a big red primary button **inside the confirmation dialog**, where it genuinely is the primary action. The red arrives at the moment it carries information, instead of shouting from a screen where the user was not going to delete anything.
80: 
81: ---
82: 
83: ## 5. LABELS ARE A LAST RESORT
84: 
85: `label: value` gives every piece of data equal weight, which is the opposite of hierarchy. It reads as a database dump because that is structurally what it is.
86: 
87: Most data identifies itself:
88: 
89: - **By format.** `$19.99` is a price. `name@example.com` is an email. `(415) 555-0132` is a phone number. A label adds nothing.
90: - **By context.** The number under a product title in a cart is a quantity.
91: 
92: Where a label is genuinely needed, in order of preference:
93: 
94: 1. **Fold it into the value.** "12 left in stock", not "In stock: 12". "3 bedrooms", not "Bedrooms: 3".
95: 2. **Make it visibly secondary.** Smaller, lighter, or both — so the eye reaches the value first.
96: 
97: The exception is a spec-sheet page, where users scan *for the label* to find the row they want. There, emphasize the label instead, because the label is what is being searched.
98: 
99: ---
100: 
101: ## 6. BALANCE WEIGHT AGAINST CONTRAST
102: 
103: Weight and contrast are interchangeable currencies, and an element that reads wrong is usually holding too much of one.
104: 
105: **Too heavy?** Reduce contrast. A solid icon covers far more surface area than the text beside it and will out-shout it at the same color; soften the icon's color to compensate. Two elements at the same nominal contrast are not equally loud if one is a solid shape and the other is text.
106: 
107: **Too faint?** Add weight. When a 1px border is too subtle in a soft color but too harsh once darkened, keep the soft color and go to 2px. The problem was never the color.
108: 
109: Stated as one rule: **add weight to fix low contrast; reduce contrast to fix excess weight.**
110: 
111: ---
112: 
113: ## 7. VISUAL HIERARCHY IS NOT DOCUMENT HIERARCHY
114: 
115: Semantic markup and visual weight are separate decisions, and conflating them produces oversized page titles everywhere.
116: 
117: Section titles are usually **labels**, not headlines. An `h1` rendered at 16px is entirely correct when the heading exists for structure and assistive technology rather than for the eye. Sometimes the title should be visually hidden altogether, because the content already says what it is and a visible heading would only add a competitor to the primary content.
118: 
119: Choose the tag for the document outline. Choose the size, weight and color for the visual tier. They are allowed to disagree.
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 8. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
124: 
125: - [`diagnosis-table.md`](diagnosis-table.md) Section 2 — the symptoms that resolve to a hierarchy failure, which is most of them.
126: - [`ux-laws.md`](ux-laws.md) Section 5 — the perceptual basis: Von Restorff for the single exception, proximity for grouping.
127: - [`../assets/token-starter-set.md`](../assets/token-starter-set.md) — which grey belongs to which text tier.

15: # Motion Principles
16: 
17: Motion is communication, not decoration. The twelve principles say what motion should express; the rules in Section 4 say what values express it.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Core Principle
24: 
25: Great animation is invisible. Users do not think "nice ease-out curve" — they think "this feels good", and they cannot say why. Motion that draws attention to itself has failed.
26: 
27: ### When to Use
28: 
29: - Adding or reviewing any transition, animation or gesture.
30: - Choosing between a spring and an easing curve.
31: - Deciding whether something should animate at all.
32: - Motion feels sluggish, chaotic, or cartoonish and the cause is unclear.
33: 
34: ### Sources
35: 
36: The twelve principles are Disney's, codified in the 1930s and adapted to interfaces by Raphael Salaja (<https://userinterface.wiki>). The enforceable rules in Section 4 are that adaptation's timing, easing, physics and staging ruleset, restated here with their values intact.
37: 
38: ### The Two Halves
39: 
40: Sections 2 and 3 are judgment — what a piece of motion is *for*. Section 4 is mechanical — values that can be checked in a diff. Read the judgment half when designing motion and the mechanical half when reviewing it.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART ONE
45: 
46: ### 1. Squash and stretch
47: 
48: Everything has mass, and momentary deformation is what tells the brain about weight, material and energy. Digital objects have no physics, so it has to be faked.
49: 
50: Keep it subtle. Too much squash and stretch turns professional software into a cartoon. The target is believability, not slapstick — see the 0.95 to 1.05 bound in Section 4.
51: 
52: ### 2. Anticipation
53: 
54: Prepare the user for what comes next. A pitcher winds up; a dancer bends before leaping. In an interface, a pull-to-refresh gesture reveals a hint as the drag passes the threshold, and the elastic resistance says something will happen on release.
55: 
56: Reserve anticipation for moments that matter. If every micro-interaction has a wind-up, the app feels sluggish. Save the drama for the dramatic.
57: 
58: ### 3. Staging
59: 
60: Anticipation is about the before; staging is about the during. When a complex panel opens, what should the eye land on first? If everything animates at once, the answer is nothing — attention scatters.
61: 
62: Bring one element into focus and dim the rest. Staging is film direction: not just showing information, but directing attention.
63: 
64: ### 4. Straight ahead action and pose to pose
65: 
66: Straight ahead means drawing frame after frame and letting the animation discover itself. Pose to pose means defining the key moments first and filling the gaps.
67: 
68: The web works pose to pose: define the keyframes and let the browser interpolate. That means nailing the important states — start, end, occasionally a midpoint — rather than obsessing over every frame.
69: 
70: It also means **not everything needs to move**. Apple's context menus animate only on exit, never on entry, because context menus are used constantly and an entrance animation would compound into irritation. Sometimes the best animation is none.
71: 
72: ### 5. Follow through and overlapping action
73: 
74: Nothing in nature moves as a rigid unit. Hair keeps moving after you stop walking; arms take a moment to catch up when you start running.
75: 
76: This is what springs are for. They add the organic overshoot-and-settle that an easing curve cannot reproduce. The danger is latency: too much stagger and the interface feels like it is thinking too hard, so keep it off critical paths.
77: 
78: ### 6. Slow in and slow out
79: 
80: Nothing starts or stops instantly. This is the cornerstone of comfortable transitions, and in practice it is the easing curve.
81: 
82: `ease-out` makes entrances feel snappy — the element arrives fast and settles gently. `ease-in` suits exits, building momentum before departure. `ease-in-out` suits deliberate movement such as a panel sliding across the screen. Linear motion reads as mechanical, which is why it is reserved for progress indicators.
83: 
84: ---
85: 
86: ## 3. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART TWO
87: 
88: ### 7. Arcs
89: 
90: Movement along a gentle curve feels organic; movement in a straight line feels mechanical. Arcs are hard to get right in UI and are most useful for hero moments and playful interactions. For utilitarian interfaces, straight lines are fine.
91: 
92: ### 8. Secondary action
93: 
94: Small flourishes that support the main action without stealing it: a checkmark that pops and then sparkles after a successful submit. The sparkle is not the message; it reinforces it. Sound can play this role too.
95: 
96: ### 9. Timing
97: 
98: Timing is the speed of an action, and it is what makes an interface feel snappy or broken. A tooltip at 150ms feels responsive; the same tooltip at 400ms feels broken. The information did not change, only the wait.
99: 
100: **Keep user-initiated interactions under 300ms.** Anything longer needs a stated reason.
101: 
102: More important than any single value: **be consistent**. If buttons animate at 200ms, every button animates at 200ms. Inconsistent timing creates a subconscious sense that something is wrong even when nobody can articulate it. Define the timing scale early and reuse it, exactly as with the spacing and type scales in `SKILL.md`.
103: 
104: ### 10. Exaggeration
105: 
106: Amplifying motion past physical accuracy to make a point land. Theatrical and intentional, and correct only in the right moments: onboarding, empty states, confirmations, error notifications. Everywhere else it is noise.
107: 
108: ### 11. Solid drawing
109: 
110: Traditional animators made 2D drawings feel three-dimensional. The translation is depth: shadows suggest it, layering implies hierarchy, and CSS `perspective` gives 3D transforms actual depth instead of flat rotation.
111: 
112: Consistency is the other half. If an icon rotates in 3D it must not suddenly read flat or inverted. This is the moving counterpart of the light-source rules in [`depth-and-detail.md`](depth-and-detail.md) Section 2 — one light source, one set of physics, held everywhere.
113: 
114: ### 12. Appeal
115: 
116: The sum of the other eleven, applied with care. Appeal is the difference between software people tolerate and software they recommend. It is not a technique; it is what happens when someone clearly gave a damn.
117: 
118: ---
119: 
120: ## 4. THE ENFORCEABLE RULESET
121: 
122: These are checkable in a diff. Grouped by what they govern.
123: 
124: ### Timing
125: 
126: | Rule | Value |
127: |---|---|
128: | User-initiated animation ceiling | 300ms; longer needs a stated reason |
129: | Press and hover | 120 to 180ms |
130: | Small state change — toggle, dropdown, tooltip | 180 to 260ms |
131: | Similar elements | identical timing values, no exceptions |
132: | Feels slow | shorten the duration before touching the curve |
133: | Context menus | no entrance animation; exit only |
134: | Stagger | under 50ms per item |
135: 
136: ### Easing and springs
137: 
138: | Situation | Use |
139: |---|---|
140: | Entrance | `ease-out` |
141: | Exit | `ease-in` |
142: | View or mode transition | `ease-in-out` |
143: | Progress or elapsed time | `linear` — and nothing else uses linear |
144: | System state change | an easing curve |
145: | Gesture-driven motion (drag, flick, swipe) | a spring |
146: | Interruptible motion | a spring |
147: | Overshoot and settle | a spring, not an easing curve |
148: | Decay of a value over time | an exponential ramp, not a linear one |
149: 
150: When a gesture ends, pass the input velocity into the spring so the release preserves the energy the user put in. Keep spring parameters balanced — `stiffness: 1000, damping: 5` oscillates like a toy; something near `stiffness: 500, damping: 30` settles.
151: 
152: ### Physics
153: 
154: - Every interactive element needs an `:active` state with a scale transform. Without one it feels unresponsive under the finger.
155: - Deformation stays in the **0.95 to 1.05** range. `scale(0.8)` on a tap is a cartoon.
156: - Animation values are proportional to the trigger size: a dialog scales from about `0.8`, a button presses to about `0.96`.
157: 
158: ### Staging
159: 
160: - One element animates prominently at a time. Two competing animations split attention and neither reads.
161: - Dim modal and dialog backgrounds rather than using a transparent overlay; a transparent scrim does not isolate anything.
162: - Animated elements need explicit `z-index`. Tooltips and overlays without one render behind content and break the layering.
163: 
164: ### When not to animate
165: 
166: - High-frequency interactions — a search input reacting to every keystroke.
167: - Keyboard navigation. Focus movement is instant; use `:focus-visible` styling, not a motion component.
168: - Context menu entrances.
169: - Theme switches, which must suppress transitions entirely for the duration of the swap.
170: 
171: ### Reduced motion
172: 
173: Honour the user's reduced-motion setting on every animation that moves content. On the web that is the `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query. On native it is the platform setting, iOS Reduce Motion or Android Remove animations, read through the platform accessibility API. Under reduced motion, replace movement with an instant change or a short opacity fade, keep essential feedback such as progress and a state change, and never auto-play motion.
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 5. RECONCILING THE DURATION GUIDANCE
178: 
179: Three sources give three ceilings, and the disagreement is real rather than a rounding difference.
180: 
181: | Source | Says |
182: |---|---|
183: | Web Interface Guidelines | not more than 200ms, for interactions to feel immediate |
184: | This ruleset | 300ms ceiling; 120 to 180ms press and hover; 180 to 260ms small state |
185: | `sk-design-md-generator` numeric design laws | 100 to 150ms feedback, 200 to 300ms state change, 300 to 500ms layout transition |
186: 
187: They are measuring different things. The 200ms figure is about *direct feedback* — the response to a press or hover, where any perceptible lag reads as unresponsiveness. The 300ms ceiling is about *user-initiated state changes*, which are allowed slightly more room because something visibly changed. The 300 to 500ms band covers *layout transitions* such as a drawer or modal, which are not blocking a further input.
188: 
189: Use this resolution:
190: 
191: - **Direct feedback** — press, hover, tap: 120 to 180ms. Never above 200ms.
192: - **State change** — toggle, dropdown, tooltip, tab: 180 to 260ms. Never above 300ms.
193: - **Layout transition** — modal, drawer, accordion: up to 500ms, and only when it is not blocking the next input.
194: - **One earned entrance** per surface may run 500 to 800ms. Repeated page-load choreography is not earned.
195: 
196: The consistency rule outranks all of these. A single value reused everywhere beats a perfectly-tuned value used once.
197: 
198: ---
199: 
200: ## 6. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
201: 
202: - [`interaction-craft.md`](interaction-craft.md) Section 6 — the implementation-level motion items: theme swaps, off-screen loops, smooth anchors.
203: - [`depth-and-detail.md`](depth-and-detail.md) Section 2 — the static light-source model that Solid Drawing extends into motion.
204: - [`review-checklist.md`](review-checklist.md) — how these rules surface in an audit pass.

40: Sections 2 and 3 are judgment — what a piece of motion is *for*. Section 4 is mechanical — values that can be checked in a diff. Read the judgment half when designing motion and the mechanical half when reviewing it.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 2. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART ONE
45: 
46: ### 1. Squash and stretch
47: 
48: Everything has mass, and momentary deformation is what tells the brain about weight, material and energy. Digital objects have no physics, so it has to be faked.
49: 
50: Keep it subtle. Too much squash and stretch turns professional software into a cartoon. The target is believability, not slapstick — see the 0.95 to 1.05 bound in Section 4.
51: 
52: ### 2. Anticipation
53: 
54: Prepare the user for what comes next. A pitcher winds up; a dancer bends before leaping. In an interface, a pull-to-refresh gesture reveals a hint as the drag passes the threshold, and the elastic resistance says something will happen on release.
55: 
56: Reserve anticipation for moments that matter. If every micro-interaction has a wind-up, the app feels sluggish. Save the drama for the dramatic.
57: 
58: ### 3. Staging
59: 
60: Anticipation is about the before; staging is about the during. When a complex panel opens, what should the eye land on first? If everything animates at once, the answer is nothing — attention scatters.
61: 
62: Bring one element into focus and dim the rest. Staging is film direction: not just showing information, but directing attention.
63: 
64: ### 4. Straight ahead action and pose to pose
65: 
66: Straight ahead means drawing frame after frame and letting the animation discover itself. Pose to pose means defining the key moments first and filling the gaps.
67: 
68: The web works pose to pose: define the keyframes and let the browser interpolate. That means nailing the important states — start, end, occasionally a midpoint — rather than obsessing over every frame.
69: 
70: It also means **not everything needs to move**. Apple's context menus animate only on exit, never on entry, because context menus are used constantly and an entrance animation would compound into irritation. Sometimes the best animation is none.
71: 
72: ### 5. Follow through and overlapping action
73: 
74: Nothing in nature moves as a rigid unit. Hair keeps moving after you stop walking; arms take a moment to catch up when you start running.
75: 
76: This is what springs are for. They add the organic overshoot-and-settle that an easing curve cannot reproduce. The danger is latency: too much stagger and the interface feels like it is thinking too hard, so keep it off critical paths.
77: 
78: ### 6. Slow in and slow out
79: 
80: Nothing starts or stops instantly. This is the cornerstone of comfortable transitions, and in practice it is the easing curve.
81: 
82: `ease-out` makes entrances feel snappy — the element arrives fast and settles gently. `ease-in` suits exits, building momentum before departure. `ease-in-out` suits deliberate movement such as a panel sliding across the screen. Linear motion reads as mechanical, which is why it is reserved for progress indicators.
83: 
84: ---
85: 
86: ## 3. THE TWELVE PRINCIPLES, PART TWO
87: 
88: ### 7. Arcs
89: 
90: Movement along a gentle curve feels organic; movement in a straight line feels mechanical. Arcs are hard to get right in UI and are most useful for hero moments and playful interactions. For utilitarian interfaces, straight lines are fine.
91: 
92: ### 8. Secondary action
93: 
94: Small flourishes that support the main action without stealing it: a checkmark that pops and then sparkles after a successful submit. The sparkle is not the message; it reinforces it. Sound can play this role too.
95: 
96: ### 9. Timing
97: 
98: Timing is the speed of an action, and it is what makes an interface feel snappy or broken. A tooltip at 150ms feels responsive; the same tooltip at 400ms feels broken. The information did not change, only the wait.
99: 
100: **Keep user-initiated interactions under 300ms.** Anything longer needs a stated reason.
101: 
102: More important than any single value: **be consistent**. If buttons animate at 200ms, every button animates at 200ms. Inconsistent timing creates a subconscious sense that something is wrong even when nobody can articulate it. Define the timing scale early and reuse it, exactly as with the spacing and type scales in `SKILL.md`.
103: 
104: ### 10. Exaggeration
105: 
106: Amplifying motion past physical accuracy to make a point land. Theatrical and intentional, and correct only in the right moments: onboarding, empty states, confirmations, error notifications. Everywhere else it is noise.
107: 
108: ### 11. Solid drawing
109: 
110: Traditional animators made 2D drawings feel three-dimensional. The translation is depth: shadows suggest it, layering implies hierarchy, and CSS `perspective` gives 3D transforms actual depth instead of flat rotation.
111: 
112: Consistency is the other half. If an icon rotates in 3D it must not suddenly read flat or inverted. This is the moving counterpart of the light-source rules in [`depth-and-detail.md`](depth-and-detail.md) Section 2 — one light source, one set of physics, held everywhere.
113: 
114: ### 12. Appeal
115: 
116: The sum of the other eleven, applied with care. Appeal is the difference between software people tolerate and software they recommend. It is not a technique; it is what happens when someone clearly gave a damn.
117: 
118: ---
119: 
120: ## 4. THE ENFORCEABLE RULESET
121: 
122: These are checkable in a diff. Grouped by what they govern.
123: 
124: ### Timing
125: 
126: | Rule | Value |
127: |---|---|
128: | User-initiated animation ceiling | 300ms; longer needs a stated reason |
129: | Press and hover | 120 to 180ms |
130: | Small state change — toggle, dropdown, tooltip | 180 to 260ms |
131: | Similar elements | identical timing values, no exceptions |
132: | Feels slow | shorten the duration before touching the curve |
133: | Context menus | no entrance animation; exit only |
134: | Stagger | under 50ms per item |
135: 
136: ### Easing and springs
137: 
138: | Situation | Use |
139: |---|---|
140: | Entrance | `ease-out` |
141: | Exit | `ease-in` |
142: | View or mode transition | `ease-in-out` |
143: | Progress or elapsed time | `linear` — and nothing else uses linear |
144: | System state change | an easing curve |
145: | Gesture-driven motion (drag, flick, swipe) | a spring |
146: | Interruptible motion | a spring |
147: | Overshoot and settle | a spring, not an easing curve |
148: | Decay of a value over time | an exponential ramp, not a linear one |
149: 
150: When a gesture ends, pass the input velocity into the spring so the release preserves the energy the user put in. Keep spring parameters balanced — `stiffness: 1000, damping: 5` oscillates like a toy; something near `stiffness: 500, damping: 30` settles.
151: 
152: ### Physics
153: 
154: - Every interactive element needs an `:active` state with a scale transform. Without one it feels unresponsive under the finger.
155: - Deformation stays in the **0.95 to 1.05** range. `scale(0.8)` on a tap is a cartoon.
156: - Animation values are proportional to the trigger size: a dialog scales from about `0.8`, a button presses to about `0.96`.
157: 
158: ### Staging
159: 
160: - One element animates prominently at a time. Two competing animations split attention and neither reads.
161: - Dim modal and dialog backgrounds rather than using a transparent overlay; a transparent scrim does not isolate anything.
162: - Animated elements need explicit `z-index`. Tooltips and overlays without one render behind content and break the layering.
163: 
164: ### When not to animate
165: 
166: - High-frequency interactions — a search input reacting to every keystroke.
167: - Keyboard navigation. Focus movement is instant; use `:focus-visible` styling, not a motion component.
168: - Context menu entrances.
169: - Theme switches, which must suppress transitions entirely for the duration of the swap.
170: 
171: ### Reduced motion
172: 
173: Honour the user's reduced-motion setting on every animation that moves content. On the web that is the `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query. On native it is the platform setting, iOS Reduce Motion or Android Remove animations, read through the platform accessibility API. Under reduced motion, replace movement with an instant change or a short opacity fade, keep essential feedback such as progress and a state change, and never auto-play motion.
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 5. RECONCILING THE DURATION GUIDANCE
178: 
179: Three sources give three ceilings, and the disagreement is real rather than a rounding difference.
180: 
181: | Source | Says |
182: |---|---|
183: | Web Interface Guidelines | not more than 200ms, for interactions to feel immediate |
184: | This ruleset | 300ms ceiling; 120 to 180ms press and hover; 180 to 260ms small state |
185: | `sk-design-md-generator` numeric design laws | 100 to 150ms feedback, 200 to 300ms state change, 300 to 500ms layout transition |
186: 
187: They are measuring different things. The 200ms figure is about *direct feedback* — the response to a press or hover, where any perceptible lag reads as unresponsiveness. The 300ms ceiling is about *user-initiated state changes*, which are allowed slightly more room because something visibly changed. The 300 to 500ms band covers *layout transitions* such as a drawer or modal, which are not blocking a further input.
188: 
189: Use this resolution:
190: 
191: - **Direct feedback** — press, hover, tap: 120 to 180ms. Never above 200ms.
192: - **State change** — toggle, dropdown, tooltip, tab: 180 to 260ms. Never above 300ms.
193: - **Layout transition** — modal, drawer, accordion: up to 500ms, and only when it is not blocking the next input.
194: - **One earned entrance** per surface may run 500 to 800ms. Repeated page-load choreography is not earned.
195: 
196: The consistency rule outranks all of these. A single value reused everywhere beats a perfectly-tuned value used once.
197: 
198: ---
199: 
200: ## 6. REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
201: 
202: - [`interaction-craft.md`](interaction-craft.md) Section 6 — the implementation-level motion items: theme swaps, off-screen loops, smooth anchors.
203: - [`depth-and-detail.md`](depth-and-detail.md) Section 2 — the static light-source model that Solid Drawing extends into motion.
204: - [`review-checklist.md`](review-checklist.md) — how these rules surface in an audit pass.
